en: *Annotated Record of the Meaning of the Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Fazang of Xisi Temple in Weiguo, Jingzhao Prefecture.
Now, the True Mind is vast and empty; it transcends words and images, like casting away the trap and the snare. It is profound, silent, and beyond perception; it is devoid of—
The object and wisdom, as subject and object,
are neither born nor extinguished;
they are not transmuted by the four marks of conditioned existence.
It neither goes nor comes;
throughout the three periods of time, nothing can alter it.
It takes non-abiding as its very nature.
Branching out according to various schools,
they rise or sink following delusion and enlightenment;
arising and ceasing as they are subject to causes and conditions.
Although they may arise profusely and leap forth with vigor,
they have never stirred the source of the mind;
it remains tranquil, serene, and profoundly still.
It has never deviated from the law of karmic cause and effect;
thus, while the nature remains unchanging, the defiled and the pure arise through conditions and remain eternally distinct.
Yet, without abandoning conditions, one is immediately the Truth, so that ordinary beings and sages reach a state of oneness.
It is like waves, which are not different from the movement of water;
thus one distinguishes the waves by means of the water.
Water, in turn, has no movement other than its own flow.
Thus, the waves are clarified through the water;
in this way, movement and stillness mutually penetrate,
and the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously fused.
Samsara and Nirvana share the same thread as Yi Yin and Qi Ji;
it is simply that while the Tathagata dwells in the world,
the faculties [of beings] are matured and easily disciplined.
Everything he received from the Honored One’s words corresponded perfectly with them;
yet after the Great Master passed away,
divergent interpretations became muddled and proliferated.
Some have taken to deviant paths,
while others have rushed down narrow byways;
consequently, the precious treasures within their own homes cannot relieve the destitution of those who are solitary and impoverished.
A bright pearl within one's clothing, yet failing to realize one’s poverty and thus engaging in hired labor;
furthermore, regarding the profound purport of the Mahāyāna,
it remains submerged in the *palm-leaf* manuscripts without being sought.
The multitude of sentient beings are like a blind company,
racing along divergent paths with no thought of returning.
Then there appeared a Great Being.
His title was Maming;
he lamented this collapse of the moral order and mourned this sinking into ruin.
Now, wishing to reveal the wondrous purport of the profound sutras and once again illuminate the dim pathways,
I shall cast away the distorted vision of heterodox views and cause all to return to the correct course. Thus,
those who seek to return to the source may do so immediately, for their restoration to the fundamental is not remote.
He composed a voluminous treatise at that time,
which brought distant benefit to all classes of beings; yet, as its text was extensive and its meaning profound, [it remained difficult to grasp].
This is not something that can be fathomed by those of shallow learning;
lamenting the delusion of those in the final age,
I have again composed this treatise.
It may be said that its meaning is abundant while its phrasing is concise;
it encompasses both understanding and practice,
serving as a guide for those of middle and inferior capacities.
It is through this that one awakens and enters [the truth].
Now, "Great" (Mahā) takes inclusion as its meaning;
"Vehicle" (Yāna) takes transport as its function.
Arising refers to the mind being stirred in response to an object;
faith is decisiveness regarding its conditions. Thus, through repeated inquiry and refutation, one arrives at certainty.
Therefore, it is called a *śāstra*.
Thus, it is titled the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
Other meanings will be distinguished separately below.
In order to explain this treatise,
I shall briefly open ten sections.
First, distinguishing the causes for the arising of the teaching.
Second, what is subsumed within the various treasuries;
third, the scope and limits of the revealed teachings;
and fourth, the capacities of the sentient beings for whom the teachings are intended.
Fifth, the nature of the teaching as the expressive medium;
sixth, the fundamental tenets and purport as that which is expressed;
seventh, the title of the commentary.
Eight, the time and occasion of the treatise's composition;
nine, the dates of its translation;
ten, the word-by-word commentary.
First, regarding the causes for the arising of the teaching, there are briefly ten causes. The first is:
based upon what kind of wisdom?
Second, what dharma is shown;
third, how it is shown;
fourth, by what means it is manifested.
Fifth, upon what basis does it rely?
Sixth, by what power does it depend?
Seventh, for what purpose is it intended?
8. By what conditions?
9. From what does it arise?
10. To what extent is there benefit?
Regarding what kind of wisdom he initially relies upon:
it refers to the wisdom of the author of the treatise, who has deeply realized the source of the mind,
as well as his skillful and marvelous eloquence that adapts to the capacities of beings.
The *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
There are three kinds of praise for eloquence (*pratibhāna*):
first, true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).
That is to say: first, because it is untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*);
second, because its essential nature is the accomplishment of immeasurable meanings and eloquence;
third, because it is the accomplishment of the meaning of the syllables of the fruit.
Furthermore, because it is accomplished through the meaning of the words "smooth," "sharp," "superior," and "excellent.
The commentary states:
this first [element] takes fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) as its basis.
The second is that post-attainment wisdom serves as the cause;
the third is that verbal teaching serves as the result.
Therefore, the arising of the teaching depends internally upon wisdom.
Second, as for what dharma is shown:
it is the one mind and the two gates.
The three greatnesses,
the four faiths,
and the five practices and so forth.
This is precisely the teaching for giving rise to faith within the Mahāyāna;
this is what has been shown. Third, how is it shown?
That is to say, by means of skillful means, the single flavor of the Mahāyāna is opened up into two types:
the letter (dharma) and the meaning (artha);
thus, the one mind-dharma is divided.
Furthermore, two gates are established to analyze a single principle,
which is further divided into three great sections.
By means of this skillfulness, one attains elucidation.
Fourth, by what is it manifested?
It is manifested by means of exquisite sounds, excellent syllables, analogies, propositions, and logical reasons.
This causes the principles and meanings to become clear and manifest.
Fifth, upon what basis does it rely?
It relies on the sacred word of the Buddha.
And it is based on correct reasoning and authoritative means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for what power these six rely upon:
That is to say, one takes refuge in the Triple Gem,
invokes their power and requests their empowerment,
and relies upon that supreme strength.
Because there is conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*),
one is able to compose a treatise (*śāstra*). Seventh, for what purpose?
That is to say: assisting the Buddha to propagate his transformation,
crushing the heterodox to manifest the orthodox,
and protecting and upholding the bequeathed Dharma.
To cause [the Dharma] to abide long in the world,
in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Eighth, as for the causal conditions:
That is to say, this treatise was composed because [the author] took sentient beings as his object of focus, desiring to cause them to be free from all suffering and to attain ultimate happiness.
Ninth, from what does it arise?
This means that because the Bodhisattva’s great compassion is internally integrated and he pities sentient beings who have long been deluded,
he has composed this treatise to bestow the gift of Dharma upon all classes of beings.
Regarding what little benefit there is,
there are briefly six types:
first, those who have not yet developed faith.
First, to cause those who have not yet developed faith to do so;
second, to enable those who already possess faith to attain the wisdom derived from hearing.
Third, for those who have already heard it,
so that they may attain the wisdom of reflection;
fourth, for those who have already reflected and understood it.
It is for the purpose of enabling the cultivation of wisdom;
and fifth, it is for the purpose of enabling those who have already practiced to realize and enter [the fruit].
Sixth, for those who have already entered [the path],
it is for the sake of bringing them to full completion.
Briefly stated, there are these ten causal conditions.
There are further six causes for the arising of this teaching,
as stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 64:
One who wishes to compose a treatise must possess six causes. First,
it is because one desires that the meaning of the Dharma shall be widely disseminated.
Second, it is because sentient beings with various inclinations and understandings may,
by means of this causal condition,
each be able to enter the True Dharma accordingly.
Third, it is for the purpose of re-opening and clarifying various lost or obscured points of meaning.
Fourth, it is because one wishes to concisely synthesize meanings that are extensive and scattered.
Fifth, it is for the purpose of manifesting the profoundly deep meaning;
sixth, it is because one desires to inspire pure faith by adorning the meaning of the Dharma with various kinds of exquisite and beautiful words and phrases.
This treatise includes the eight causes and conditions and so forth from below,
as well as the *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, among others.
Each has its own causes and conditions,
which may be sought out and understood from them.
Second, regarding the delimitation of what is included within the Pitakas, there are two parts.
Initially, because there are three [aspects] to be expressed,
the teaching is threefold; subsequently,
because there are two [aspects] for whom it is intended, [it is twofold].
The teachings are twofold;
within the former, the three trainings (*śikṣā*) are elucidated, and thus the Three Piṭakas are established.
The first is the Sūtra Piṭaka.
Some call it *sūtra*, others call it *sūtrānta*,
and so forth; these are all Sanskrit names used according to their appropriate linguistic forms.
It is difficult to find a literal equivalent for this term; it is translated here as "Sūtra" (契經),
meaning that it accords with the truth and is suited to the capacities of sentient beings.
It is called a "seal" (kṣānti) because it pierces through and sews together;
this is designated as a "sūtra."
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
Because it penetrates, encompasses, and sustains both the meanings to be explained and the sentient beings for whom they are intended,
it is called *sūtra*.
It refers to the teaching that explains meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the *sūtra* is itself the *piṭaka*. This is an example of the *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound.
The second is called the Vinaya-piṭaka;
it is also referred to as the Vinaya or the Vinīti.
In ancient translations, this was termed "extinction" (nirodha).
This refers to the evils of body, speech, and mind;
they incinerate the practitioner, and thus their meaning is identical to that of a blazing fire.
Precepts are able to cease and extinguish [afflictions];
therefore they are called "cessation" (nirodha) or "coolness" (śītalatā).
Because it can extinguish the signs of evil and blazing heat,
it is now translated as "taming" (*dānta*).
That is to say, "taming" (*diào*) means "harmonizing."
"Vowing" (*ava*) means to subdue;
that is, to harmonize and control the actions of body, speech, and mind,
thereby restraining and eliminating all unwholesome conduct.
Discipline is this practice;
it is the very conduct of precepts that is expressed,
the treasury of discipline.
This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (possessive compound), because it is named after that which it denotes.
There are three Abhidharma Piṭakas.
Some call it *Abhidharma*.
The ancient translation was "Incomparable Dharma" (*wubifa*),
meaning that *abhi* signifies "incomparable."
Dharma is called "dharma" because it is non-conceptual wisdom that discerns the characteristics of phenomena;
since there is no other phenomenon capable of being compared to it, it is so named.
It is called the "Incomparable Dharma" (*Abhidharma*).
It is now translated as "Counter-Dharma" (*Duìfǎ*).
This means that *abhi* refers to the "counter-intellect" (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*).
Dharma refers to the phenomena that serve as objects of cognition;
that is to say, through right wisdom,
one thoroughly exhausts the source of all phenomena.
He discerns the characteristics of phenomena with such clarity that they are as distinct as one's own palms,
as if seeing them face-to-face.
Therefore, it is called Abhidharma.
Abhidharma is the wisdom that is the subject to be explained;
it is the treasury of Abhidharma.
This is also an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent determinative compound), named after that which it characterizes.
Furthermore, it may also be called the "subduing dharma," the "discriminating dharma," the "enumerated dharma," the "pervasive dharma," the "great dharma," and so forth.
And they follow their names according to their meaning, as explained elsewhere.
Question: If these three piṭakas each designate one of the three trainings, [how is this so?]
Why is it that the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, chapter eleven, states:
"Furthermore, the Sūtras are established to reveal the three trainings;
the Vinaya is so named because it reveals ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*")?
The exposition of the training in wisdom is called Abhidharma.
Answer: If one relies on the perspective of their essential nature, as previously stated, each term individually denotes a single [training].
If one follows the approach that combines both the primary and secondary categories, then as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*,
because the sūtras are broad, all three [categories] are present.
The Vinaya possesses both [the aspects of root and branch],
while the Abhidharma is narrow, possessing only one;
this is also the gate of root and branch.
That is to say, the Sūtras are the root;
the other two [Pitakas] are the branches and the end.
This treatise, among those three Piṭakas, [belongs to the Abhidharma].
Included within the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Question: As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 81:
"That is to say, the various sūtras..."
Circulating through and scrutinizing the *mātṛkā*,
such as all the sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
All are called *mātṛkā*.
This means that in these instances, the World-Honored One himself extensively analyzed the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
According to this textual evidence:
Even though the Abhidharma-piṭaka is also the word of the Buddha,
this treatise was composed by a bodhisattva after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa.
How can it also be included and categorized within the Dharma-piṭaka?
The answer is that there are two meanings.
First, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Because they belong to that same category,
they are included therein;
the second point follows the Mahāmāyā-sūtra.
The Buddha stated that Aśvaghoṣa skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma.
Since it is said he "skillfully expounds," this means his teachings are sealed by the Tathāgata’s prophetic authorization.
Thus, it should be known that this [teaching] may also be included within this treasury.
Based on this general discussion,
the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma consists of three types.
First, the Buddha speaks himself;
second, he causes others to speak;
third, he grants permission for them to speak.
This treatise shall indeed be explained by way of prior concession (*abhyupagama*).
Second, because it is twofold in terms of its intended audience,
the teaching is established as being for two purposes.
However, because faculties range from sharp to dull and dharmas range from shallow to profound,
the Tripiṭaka is divided into two categories.
Therefore, the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Treatise on Exposition), chapter four,
states: "Because of the distinction between the higher and lower vehicles,
this Piṭaka is further described as the Śrāvaka-piṭaka and the Bodhisattva-piṭaka."
Question:
Why are those three and two called "piṭakas" (baskets)?
Answer: Because they comprise [all teachings].
This means that it encompasses all objects of knowledge.
The commentary explains:

"Therefore, for those śrāvakas of dull faculties who belong to the Lesser Vehicle (hīnayāna) and engage in conceptualization based on the clinging to phenomena (dharmagrāha)," [the teaching is given].
The establishment of the Tripiṭaka that elucidates the principles, practices, and fruits of the Śrāvakas is called the Śrāvaka-piṭaka.
For the sake of bodhisattvas of sharp faculties and the supreme vehicle, who rely on the wisdom of the three natures and two selflessnesses,
the Three Pitakas are established to elucidate and demonstrate the principles, practices, stages, and fruits of the bodhisattva path.
It is called the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
Question: Since the sūtras explain the dharma of dependent origination for the sake of all pratyekabuddhas, why is the name "piṭaka" not established for the Pratyekabuddhas alone?
Answer: If one follows the *Samantabhadrotsāha-samādhi-sūtra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*, the Three Piṭakas are established in relation to the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
Now, however, we rely on the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* and the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
Because they are divided into two collections (piṭaka) according to the Great and Small Vehicles, [the Abhidharma] is not established [as a separate collection].
Question: Why do the two teachings differ regarding what is excluded or established?
Answer: These Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas share both similarities and differences.
That is to say, regarding their teachings and practices, there are slight differences, such that the Piṭakas of the three vehicles are distinguished.
Because their principles and fruits are entirely non-distinct,
they are combined into a single Piṭaka;
that is to say, they are identical in severing the grasping at a self and identical in realizing the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Since their fruition is identical to that of the Arhat,
they are not established separately.
Therefore, the sūtras and śāstras differ in how they expand upon or condense these categories.
Thus, this treatise is subsumed within the Bodhisattva Piṭaka among the two Piṭakas.
Third, regarding the classification of the manifest teaching (nītārtha),
there are two parts therein.
First, the various teachings are enumerated;
subsequently, the tenets are distinguished according to those teachings.
Within the former section, the masters of this land have established their teachings and opened their schools with such profusion that they are manifold and confused.
It is difficult to describe in full detail;
I shall briefly outline ten schools as found in the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra).
Furthermore, regarding the translation of scriptures in ancient times,
this refers to the systems of doctrinal classification established by the Tripitaka masters who came from the West.
There are also many approaches;
here, five schools are briefly cited,
as explained in that [text].
Now, the Tripiṭaka Master Śīlabhadra from Central India— whose name means "Sunlight" (Rizhao) in the language of Tang—
is translating [texts] at this monastery.
I personally inquired about this, and he said:
"In recent times at Nālandā Monastery in India..."
At that time, there were two great virtuous masters of debate:
one was named Śīlabhadra,
and the other was named Jñānaprabha.
His divine understanding surpassed all his contemporaries;
his fame resounded throughout the Five Indias,
and the six heretical teachers bowed their heads in submission.
Factions of different schools turned to him with sincere devotion;
Mahāyāna students looked up to him as they do to the sun and moon.
He walked alone and peerless throughout India.
Each has but a single person [as its founder].
Consequently, the lineages they inherited differ,
and the teachings they established contradict one another.
That is to say, Śīlabhadra inherited from afar the lineage of Maitreya and Asaṅga,
and followed closely upon the footsteps of Dharmapāla and Sthiramati;
he relied upon such sūtras as the Saṃdhinirmocana and treatises such as the Yogācārabhūmi.
He established three types of teachings,
regarding the Dharma-character Mahāyāna as the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
That is to say, the Buddha first turned the wheel of the Dharma of the Hīnayāna Four Truths at the Deer Park.
It is taught that all conditioned phenomena arise from conditions in order to refute the non-Buddhists' [assertion of] causes such as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, because they arise from conditions, there is no self (*pudgala*).
This overturns the claims of those non-Buddhists who assert the existence of a self (*ātman*) and so forth;
however, it has not yet explained the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*),
as found in the *Catuṣ-āgama* and other such scriptures.
During the second period,
although it relies upon the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*),
it is taught that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is entirely empty.
This overturns that Hīnayāna [view];
yet, regarding the dependent and the perfected natures,
it has not yet asserted their existence.
That is, the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and others;
during the third period,
according to the correct principles of the Mahāyāna.
Only by fully explaining the three natures, the three absences of nature, and so forth,
can one exhaustively realize the principle;
this is precisely what is taught in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other such texts.
Therefore, regarding those phenomena produced through causes and conditions,
to initially assert that they "exist" alone is to fall into the extreme of eternalism.
Next, if one speaks only of emptiness,
one falls into the extreme of emptiness. Since each has fallen into an extreme, [they are both mistaken].
Neither of these is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
At a later time, it will be fully explained that the nature of what is grasped is empty,
while the other two exist.
Only when one accords with the Middle Way can it be considered definitive;
this is judged according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
The Master Jñānaprabha inherited the lineage from afar from Mañjuśrī and Nāgārjuna,
and received instruction more recently from Āryadeva and Bhāviveka;
he relied upon the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras and the Madhyamaka treatises.
They also establish three teachings,
clarifying that the signless Mahāyāna is the true definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This refers to the Buddha’s initial teaching of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park for those of lesser faculties.
He clarifies that both mind and objects exist.
Subsequently, during the middle period,
he teaches the Dharma-character Mahāyāna to those of middling faculties.
This explains the principle of the emptiness of objects and the existence of mind-only through consciousness;
such a statement was made because their faculties were still inferior and they had not yet been able to enter the equal, true emptiness.
This refers to the third period.
For those of the highest faculties, he taught the signless Mahāyāna,
discerning that both mind and objects are empty;
this equality of a single flavor is the definitive meaning.
Furthermore, at the outset, one gradually refutes the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and other such tenets of the non-Buddhists;
therefore, it is taught that phenomena produced by causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*) definitely exist.
Subsequently, one gradually refutes the Small Vehicle's (*Hīnayāna*) attachment to the real existence of dependently arisen phenomena.
Therefore, it is said that they exist provisionally based on other-dependent causes and conditions; because they fear this true emptiness,
they are guided by means of provisional existence.
It is only at a later stage that one finally attains the ultimate Mahāyāna;
therein it is taught that this dependent origination is itself emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*), equal and of a single characteristic.
For this reason, the Dharma-characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) Mahāyāna and its systems of objective apprehension (*upalambha*) are thereby judged [to be inferior].
This is the second period, which is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
This sequence of the three teachings is as explained by the Master Jñānaprabha in his *Prajñāpradīpa-ṭīkā*.
Citing the *Mahāyāna-sūkṣma-jñāna-sūtra*,
it asks: Since these two teachings each represent the word of the Sage, they appear to be mutually contradictory.
I do not yet understand whether these two explanations can be reconciled.
The answer is that there are two meanings:
namely, neither reconciliation nor non-reconciliation.
From the outset, there has been no need for a syncretic assembly.
Since both are sacred teachings that benefit sentient beings according to their conditions,
why wait for a formal unification?
This refers to the *pratyātmamanuṣyasarvajanatā-siddhānta* (the teaching for individuals) among the four *siddhāntas* in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Therefore,
although there are apparent contradictions, [they are resolved].
Yet they cannot be reconciled;
this is also the "intention regarding the inclinations of sentient beings" among the four intentions explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
Within a single dharma, there may be both praise and censure;
therefore, these two explanations need not be reconciled. As for the two [statements], there is nothing that is not in accord.
In general, regarding the teaching gates established by these two,
there are two approaches: first, in terms of the breadth or narrowness of their inclusion of sentient beings.
The teachings are either complete or incomplete,
distinguished by whether they are clear or not;
these two are categorized according to the gradual progression of benefiting sentient beings.
The manifestation of principles increases or diminishes according to whether they are clearly understood or not; thus,
there are two [stages] regarding the beginning and the middle.
First, regarding the breadth or narrowness of the inclusion of sentient beings:
according to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*,
at the initial stage, he taught exclusively for those who had set out upon the Śrāvaka Vehicle.
During the second period, he taught exclusively for those who have set out upon the Mahāyāna.
These two [periods] each encompass only one type of capacity,
and thus do not fully encompass all capacities.
Therefore, each [of the previous two] is not definitive.
During the third period, it was taught universally for those setting out upon all vehicles;
herein, the gathering of capacities comprehensively encompasses all vehicles.
Therefore, it is said that [this teaching] is expounded universally for all vehicles;
because it encompasses all capacities without exception,
it alone is considered definitive in meaning (nītārtha).
Second, regarding the completeness or deficiency of the teachings according to the capacity [of the audience]: if one considers the teachings as they were received by those with such capacities,
then at the initial stage, only the Hīnayāna was taught.
The second [turning] speaks exclusively of the Mahāyāna;
the third speaks fully of all three vehicles (triyāna).
In the former two, each lacks the other's teaching, and thus they are incomplete.
Therefore, it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
The latter one, which possesses the three vehicles,
is of definitive meaning because its teaching is complete.
Based on these meanings,
the third position is therefore established as definitive;
this is the method upon which Śīlabhadra’s formulation relies for its judgment.
Within the second section, there are also two parts.
First, regarding the gradual sequence for benefiting beings:
this refers to the period when the teachings initially expounded were intended solely to enable sentient beings to attain the benefits of the Hīnayāna.
Because the benefit was not yet ultimate,
it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Although during the second period the benefit extended to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, [it was still not definitive].
However, this cannot cause those of the two vehicles who incline toward tranquility to also attain the Mahāyāna;
therefore, this teaching as well is not exhaustive of the truth.
It is during the third period that all are universally enabled to obtain the benefits of the Mahāyāna.
Even for those who have entered into quiescence, it causes them to dedicate [their merit] toward great enlightenment;
therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This alone is the one true reality."
The other two are not true.
It further says:
"If one were to transform others using the Lesser Vehicle..."
I would then fall into stinginess and greed;
this matter is not permissible.
Therefore, this teaching alone is explained as the definitive meaning (nītārtha).
Second, regarding the increase or decrease in the clarity of the principle:
first, dependent origination is taught as being substantially existent;
subsequently, dependent origination is taught as being conventionally existent.
It is only when dependent origination is subsequently explained that it is revealed as the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
What was taught in the preceding two [sections] did not fully manifest the principle;
their reconciliation with conditions was incomplete.
Therefore, it is not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

This treatise should be explained as follows: although the words and phrases of this treatise are few, they universally encompass the essential purports of all Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras.
Therefore, it is said to be "comprehensive," as it summarizes the vast sphere of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of equality; and it is said to be "profound," as it pertains to the realm of suchness.
It is called "vast" because it is the objective realm of wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*).
It is called "boundless" because its depth and vastness are without limit. Regarding the section on the Establishment of the Meaning, there are two distinct parts:
first, the conclusion of the preceding and the introduction of what follows.
Second, the formal establishment of the meaning.
This section consists of three parts.
First, the general heading followed by the specific opening.
Second, the inquiry based on the enumeration of names;
third, the discernment of characteristics based on those names.

Having already explained the section on causes and conditions, next is explained the section on establishing the doctrine. Regarding the Mahāyāna, it is said in general that there are two kinds. What are these two? First, phenomena (dharma); second, meaning (artha). Among the names, "phenomena" refers to—
It brings forth the essential nature of the Mahāyāna;
that is to say, because it is its own essence and because it is in opposition to [limited] cognition.
Because it manifests the meaning,
it is the fundamental dharma of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Its "great position" resides in the cause (*hetu*).
This applies to both the defiled and the pure.
As for "meaning" (artha), it refers to the analysis of the names and meanings of the Mahāyāna.
That is to say, for what reason is this mind the Mahāyāna?
It is because this mind internally possesses the three great meanings;
therefore, it is called "Great."
It is called a "vehicle" (*yāna*) because it possesses two modes of progression;
that is, based on the distinct principles revealed by the school's tenets,
the "Great Stage" (*mahā-bhūmi*) resides in the fruit.
It takes up only the pure.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna generally explains that there are two aspects:
namely, first, the manifestation of the essence of phenomena.
The subsequent explanation of the principles and meanings completes the summary of the subject matter. Within the "Discernment of Characteristics," there are two parts:
first, the phenomena (dharma), and second, the meanings (artha).
Within the Dharma there are also two parts:
first, the general establishment by citing the Dharma;
second, the specific establishment by opening the gates, beginning with the words "Why is this? and so forth.
Regarding what is called "Dharma," it refers to the mind of sentient beings. This consists of three phrases in total.
First, "the mind of sentient beings" identifies the essential substance of that Dharma.
That is to say, the *tathāgatagarbha* mind contains two gates: the gate of conjunction and the gate of non-conjunction;
this is because it exists in the stage of sentient beings. If it were in the stage of Buddhahood, [it would not be so].
Then there would be no meaning of "conjunction," because initial awakening is identical to the fundamental [awakening],
being nothing other than True Suchness (tathatā).
This refers precisely to the meaning as it is manifested.
Since we are now considering the stage of sentient beings who follow defilement,
both of these two gates are fully present.
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas. Next, regarding the phrase "encompassing all mundane and supramundane dharmas," this distinguishes the functional capacity of the dharma;
it is because the essential nature and characteristics of this mind are unimpeded.
Defilement and purity share the same basis;
whether following the current or reversing the flow,
it is solely this mind that undergoes transformation.
Therefore, if one follows along with defilement to constitute non-enlightenment (abodha),
it encompasses all worldly phenomena;
yet it does not encompass the unchanging fundamental enlightenment (mūla-awakening) nor the initial enlightenment (ādi-awakening) that flows back toward the source.
This subsumes supramundane dharmas;
this is still explained from the perspective of the gate of arising and ceasing.
If one were to explain it from the perspective of the gate of suchness:
Thus, through this melting and integration, the defiled and the pure are not distinct;
therefore, it universally encompasses them.
This is fully clarified in the text below.
"Based on this mind, the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed. Third, regarding "based on this mind, the meaning of the Great Vehicle is revealed," this explains the name of the Dharma;
that is, it is based upon this single-mind principle, the fundamental Dharma.
This reveals the meaning of the three greatnesses of the Mahāyāna;
therefore, this mind is designated as "Dharma. Within the specific [analysis], there are two parts:
first, the refutation of the general premise through a challenge.
The subsequent section provides a separate explanation for its establishment.

Why is this? Because the characteristic of the *tathatā* (suchness) of this mind directly reveals the essence of the Mahāyāna. Within the preceding [section], there are two intended meanings of the critique.
First, it says:
The mind encompasses both defilement and purity,
whereas the Mahāyāna is exclusively pure.
How, then, can this mind manifest the meaning of the Mahāyāna?
It is further said:
"The mind and its phenomena are one;
the meaning of the Mahāyāna is vast."
How can this mind manifest meaning? The explanation of the intent states:
although the Mahāyāna is pure, [it manifests through this mind].
Since characteristics and functions necessarily arise in relation to defilement,
they are now situated within the gate of arising and ceasing;
therein, both defilement and purity are fully contained.
Therefore, it is able to manifest [purity].
This is because at the time when defilement is abandoned, there is no longer the function of purity.
This explains the first meaning. Furthermore, although mental phenomena are unitary, [they appear as distinct].
There are two gates: within the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), the essence of the Mahāyāna is revealed;
within the gate of Arising and Ceasing, the three great aspects of the school are fully present.
The meaning of the Mahāyāna does not exceed these three.
Therefore, by relying on this single mind, the meaning of the three greatnesses (mahattva) is revealed.
This is established within the section on distinct gates.
The phrase "this mind as suchness" (cittatathatā) generally refers to the gate of suchness (tathatāmukha),
which introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "is precisely this single dharma-realm" (eka-dharmadhātu).
Regarding the "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*), this refers to the characteristic of *tathatā* (suchness).
This introduces the following passage: "Furthermore, *tathatā* is that which is based on verbal expression and conceptual discrimination," and so forth.

This characteristic of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of the mind can demonstrate the essence, characteristics, and function of the Mahāyāna itself. Regarding this "arising and ceasing of the mind":
it refers to its fluctuation in accordance with habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
This summarizes the gate of arising and ceasing,
which introduces the subsequent passage beginning with "Because it relies on the Tathāgatagarbha, there is the mind of arising and ceasing.
As for "causes and conditions":
Regarding the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing:
the subsequent passage beginning with "Furthermore, having explained the causes and conditions for arising and ceasing" follows from this.
As for the term "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa):
This refers to the state of arising and ceasing;
thus, the passage beginning with "Next, as for the characteristics of arising and ceasing" follows below.
For what reason is it said that [this] is "immediately shown" within the Gate of True Suchness?
Regarding the phrase "that which can manifest" within the gate of arising and ceasing:
because True Suchness is the gate of non-arising,
it possesses no distinct characteristic from the Greatness of Essence (dharmatā) revealed therein.
Because the essential meaning is not different,
it is said that this is "directly revealing.
This is because [the mind] does not arise.
This merely indicates the essence.
Arising and ceasing constitute the gate of activity;
since defilement and purity are distinct, [the essence remains constant].
The explanation of the essential meaning is further divided;
because the subject and object are not identical, it is not said that they are "identical.
As for the self-nature, characteristics, and function:
"Essence" refers to the meaning of original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) within the gate of arising and ceasing.
Because it is the self-substance of arising and ceasing and the cause of arising and ceasing,
it is also distinguished as the essence within the gate of arising and ceasing.
The pure aspect of transformative defilement and the functional activity of conformative defilement both reside within this gate; therefore,
they are discussed in full detail here.
Therefore, the subsequent passage explains the section on the gate of arising and ceasing,
fully manifesting the meaning of the three greatnesses (mahā) thus indicated;
this is the intended purport.
Why is it that in the gate of True Suchness (*tathatā*) one speaks directly of "essence" (*tattva*),
whereas in the gate of arising and ceasing one speaks of "intrinsic essence" (*svabhāva*) and so forth?
It is because the three great meanings being demonstrated still reside within the gate of arising and ceasing, which serves as the means of demonstration.
This reveals that it is not something separate or external;
therefore, it is called "self.
Question: True Suchness is the gate of non-arising.
Regarding the mere indication of the essence (*tattva*):
since arising and ceasing are gates of movement and activity,
one should indicate only the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and functions (*vṛtti*).
Answer: True Suchness (tathatā) is the gate of non-arising.
This non-arising does not necessarily depend upon the establishment of arising; it is because there is no arising at all.
Therefore, only the essence is shown.
Arising and ceasing are the gate of activation;
arising necessarily relies upon non-arising.
Since arising includes non-arising,
the three greatnesses are fully contained within arising.
The remainder is as explained below.
Regarding the phrase "The meaning of the ultimate nature of phenomena is vast":
this introduces the following section, beginning with "Furthermore, as for the self-substance and characteristics of True Suchness," and so forth.
This section contains two parts.
First, the "Great" (Mahāyāna) is distinguished;
subsequently, the "Vehicle" (Yāna) is explained.
Within the former, there are also two parts.
First the heading, then the explanation.

Regarding what is called "meaning" (*artha*), there are three kinds. What are these three? First is the greatness of essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*), which refers to the fact that the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing. In the explanation, there are three [parts].
Regarding the primary essence:
its true nature is profound and vast;
it serves as the basis for all ordinary beings and sages, as well as for both defilement and purity.
Therefore, it receives its great name:
though followed by the flow of defilements, it does not increase;
though reversed from the flow to eliminate defilements, it does not decrease.
Furthermore, when returning to the source, it is augmented by purity without increase;
when following the flow, it lacks purity without decrease.
This is truly because neither defilement nor purity causes any deficiency.
Because it is that which remains unchanging from beginning to end, it is said to be equal, without increase or decrease.

Second is the greatness of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahātmya*), meaning that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fully endowed with immeasurable inherent merits. Regarding the greatness of its characteristics:
Regarding the meaning of non-emptiness within the two kinds of Tathāgatagarbha,
it refers to the characteristic of being non-different from the essence; therefore,
it is called "intrinsic virtue" (prakṛti-guṇa).

Just as the eight qualities of water are not different from the water itself, the third is the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahattva*), because it is able to produce all mundane and supramundane causes and effects of goodness. Regarding the greatness of function:
This refers to the spontaneous great function of illusory manifestation according to defiled karma;
it is the coarse and subtle functions of the two bodies of retribution and transformation,
which cause all sentient beings to first accomplish worldly goodness and ultimately achieve transcendence.
The following text clarifies this.
Why is it that only "wholesome" is mentioned, and not "unwholesome"?
Because unwholesome dharmas contradict reality and are that which is to be remedied,
they do not constitute its function.
If that were so, all unwholesome dharmas would be separated from reality.
The commentary states:
Because it contradicts reality,
one cannot be separated from reality;
because it contradicts reality...
It is not its function. [The character for "vehicle" (*yāna*)] consists of two middle strokes.
It is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden upon. First, the fruit is indicated in relation to the cause to explain the vehicle:
because all Bodhisattvas ride this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata. Subsequently, the cause is cited in relation to the fruit to establish the conveyance.
This is because the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) is that which mounts,
while the principle of original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) is that which is mounted.
As the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
Because it rides upon the great nature, it is called the Mahāyāna.
This concludes the Section on Establishing the Meaning.
